data.title: Worse than taking away your parents' car keys? Taking away their cell phone. How to protect your aging parents.
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

Worse than taking away your parents' car keys? Taking away their cell phone. How to protect your aging parents. Parental controls aren't just for kids anymore

There are two main approaches for families to help aging loved ones who are having trouble with technology: Roll into it slowly, or just do it.

When the time came for Elliott Appel's dad to stop driving, he willingly gave up his car keys. But when Appel told him it was no longer safe for him to have unmonitored access to a computer or phone, it was a much bigger deal.

"The phone stuff was about a year and a half later than the car," said Appel, who at that point was already handling a lot of his father's financial and medical affairs, in conjunction with his mother, even though his parents were long divorced. Appel said he made the jump to restrict access to internet-connected devices because he saw some alarming irregularities: random withdrawals on his father's bank account that looked sketchy, and a check to a neighbor for $1,000. In addition to cancer and dementia, Appel's father had mental-health and addiction problems.

"I figured he's buying drugs or other things are happening, and I thought, 'How best can we prevent this?'" said Appel, who was in his 20s when he had to start taking care of his father. An opportunity came up when his father lost his phone during a hospital visit. Appel replaced it, but under his own plan, and handed it over with child-protection monitoring software installed.

"It doesn't feel good in the moment, but this was the lesser of all evils," Appel said. "It meant that we could block a number if we needed to. Then [his health] declined so much that we didn't need it later on."

Appel's father died in 2023, in his mid-70s, after about seven tumultuous years of challenging health problems. Appel is now in his mid-30s and works as a financial planner based in Wisconsin who specializes in helping families with transitions like the one his own family faced. He recently published a book on the topic titled, "How to Help Your Parents as They Age: A Financial Planner's Guide to Caregiving."

There are two main approaches for families to help aging loved ones who are having trouble with technology: Roll into it slowly, or just do it.

Appel is for doing what you have to do. "You just jump in," he said. "It's like any other caregiving task. It feels less bad the further you go along. He was actively hurting himself. He had over $1,000 in insufficient-funds fees because he wasn't keeping track of his spending."

Jen Eaves has been taking a slower approach to her mother's cognitive decline, even though she's the vice president of marketing for Aura, a family online safety company. It's one thing for people to sign up for preventive monitoring of their own accounts, and another thing for an adult child to do that for an aging parent who is trying to maintain their independence.

"Her device is how she stays connected to the world, so taking that away is the most terrifying thing," Eaves said. But the reality is that her mother had had a stroke and a series of other health problems and wasn't being safe with her internet access. There were worries about scams. There were problems with spending on suspicious health supplements. Her mom even took out a new credit card simply by inadvertently checking a box when putting through an Amazon order.

Eaves's question to her mom was: "How do I make sure you're still in control, but also talk about how you can be safe?"

The answer was monitoring software for now - and no, Eaves does not feel bad about it. "My brother is the other caregiver, and he's a lot more sensitive. I'm just like, oh, no, you need me. I'm going to make sure you're OK," she said. "Maybe at first it felt Big Brotherish, but my mom realizes now that she needs to hand this over to me."

The key to family harmony with either of these approaches is to maintain the person's dignity as much as possible, said Kate Nattoli, a certified dementia practitioner with Crescent Grove Advisors. Most of the products a family may look at are labeled as "child protection," and that brings home the role reversals involved in parenting your parents. "It's wonky territory to try to navigate," said Nattoli. "You want to make sure everyone knows you're coming from a place of love and care and concern. Say, 'I want to be a support to you, not control you.'"

Most families are able to work through these issues without involving the courts. While having a power of attorney designated for a person who is suffering cognitive decline is an absolute necessity, having them declared incompetent by a court is not. The monitoring of and restricted access to devices instead should come through negotiation, even when you are dealing with someone who is very recalcitrant.

Appel thought about pursuing guardianship over his father because his situation was so complicated.

"We paid an attorney for a consult, but in the end, nothing would have changed other than a lot more bureaucracy. He was going to do whatever he was going to do," Appel said. They also thought about video monitoring in his dad's apartment when he insisted on living alone, but that was a bridge too far for all of them as far as dignity and privacy were concerned.

Surveillance may be less of a concern in other families where divorce and estrangement aren't part of the equation. Family dynamics run deep, and sorting through the complications involved in restricting a connection to the outside world or keeping tabs on an older person will look different for every household. And the icky feelings about the intrusion may persist until you have transparent conversations about it.

Just keep at it, Nattoli advises. "Be up front and forthright and make sure your intentions are well known," she said. "And the earlier the better."

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

-Beth Pinsker

data.title: Rising interest rates: The good, the bad and the ugly for retirees
data.description:
By Geoffrey Sanzenbacher

Unlike higher gas prices, which hurt almost everyone, higher borrowing costs have an uneven impact

Rising interest rates can upend the finances of some seniors.

In September 2024, Donald Trump, then the Republican nominee for president, promised: "We're going to put a temporary cap on credit-card interest rates ... at around 10%." Yet today, the Bankrate Monitor National Index shows the average credit-card APR at a historically elevated 19.6%.

Mortgage rates are also at levels not seen since the turn of the century. Those numbers are only likely to rise, as these and other interest rates often increase within a few months of hikes in the federal-funds rate - like the one that just happened last month.

Unlike higher gas prices, which hurt almost everyone, higher borrowing costs have a mixed impact - especially for older Americans. People with credit-card debt suffer. But a higher federal-funds rate also leads to higher returns on assets that retirees often hold. Given high government debt, the funding needs for the AI build-out and inflation fueled by the Iran war, interest rates are likely to remain high. It's worth a look at the various ways - good, bad and ugly - that high rates affect those near and in retirement.

Opinion: Falling wages, soaring energy prices and inflation: It's beginning to look a lot like the 1970s

The good: Annuities and cash-like assets

Higher interest rates have a few clear benefits for those near and in retirement. For near-retirees who are considering annuitizing some of their wealth, higher rates are helpful. For example, the monthly payout for a $100,000 annuity bottomed out around $425 for a 65-year-old female when interest rates fell during the COVID-19 pandemic, and have rebounded to nearly $600 a month as rates have risen. Certainly, this impact could be good news for the admittedly small (but perhaps growing) number of people who use annuities.

A more common positive impact is for those who hold cash-like assets with interest rates that respond to the federal-funds rate: mainly, savings accounts, money-market accounts and short-term certificates of deposit. Roughly 3 in 5 Americans ages 55 and over hold at least some wealth in these assets, according to an analysis of the Survey of Consumer Finances. Still, those assets are usually a small part of older Americans' net worth - 3% to 4%, on average. So while rising interest rates can help here, it may not be a huge boon.

Opinion: Here's a sneaky way to play the Fed's rate increase

The bad: Houses, bonds - and (maybe) 401(k)s

When people think of high interest rates, mortgage rates usually spring to mind. But since over 70% of people ages 55 and over already own their homes, it's natural to assume that mortgage rates don't affect them. Still, higher mortgage rates make it harder to unlock home equity by downsizing and moving to a place more amenable to retirement. For example, one study found that rises in interest rates postponed lifestyle moves to independent living communities for four to five years.

Aside from this effect, rising interest rates can also undermine certain assets held by retirees and those close to retirement. The most obvious type would be directly held bonds or bond mutual funds, whose prices tend to drop when interest rates rise. However, only about 6% of these households hold such assets.

Far more ubiquitous are bonds held indirectly, often through target-date funds in 401(k) accounts. Roughly half of households ages 55 to 64 have assets in a 401(k), and about a third of those balances are in target-date funds. Since these funds shift to bonds as people approach retirement, higher interest rates could reduce returns in many workers' 401(k)s.

Whether this happens depends a bit on how stock prices react to the higher rates - something that is more ambiguous. Still, it's worth keeping an eye on whether 401(k) returns decline at a crucial time for retirement savers. Then again, at least those with target-date funds have a pile of assets. The people really hurt by higher rates are those with a pile of debt.

The ugly: Big credit-card balances

The most vulnerable group to increasing interest rates are those who must deal with higher borrowing costs without much ability to increase their earnings. Many of these people are low income. Figure 1 below divides people ages 55 to 64 and those 65-plus into five roughly equal income groups, from low to high, and shows their credit-card debt divided by their income. A higher value indicates a higher debt burden relative to what can be afforded.

The figure shows that lower-income people have a higher debt burden than those with more money. On average, the poorest 20% of 55- to 64-year-olds (gray dashed line) hold credit-card debt equal to over 10% of their income. For those 65-plus, the number is 5% (gray solid line). The comparable numbers for the richest 20% are much lower, at around 1%.

The figure also highlights that some lower-income people are in real trouble. If you look within that poorest 20%, you'd see that 10% of people have credit-card balances worth over 20% of their income. For the richest 20%, that same number is below 5%. To the extent that recent and future federal-funds rate hikes spill over to credit cards, low-income people will be hit the hardest.

I've written in this space before about how the Trump administration's policies have either hurt the vulnerable or disproportionately helped the rich. While higher interest rates aren't a policy aim of the administration - indeed, the White House has agitated for lower rates - its policies have led to higher rates. By passing a large tax cut and following it up with a costly war, the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is at near-record highs despite an economic expansion.

Relief on interest rates likely isn't coming, and the ugly truth is that the most likely group to be hurt is already low income.

-Geoffrey Sanzenbacher

data.title: Verda Healthcare, Inc. and AstranaCare Partners Form a Multi-State Partnership
data.description:
Verda Healthcare, Inc. and AstranaCare Partners Form a Multi-State Partnership

Verda Healthcare, Inc. is proud to announce a new partnership with AstranaCare Partners of Arizona and AstranaCare Partners of Texas. AstranaCare, through a large network of Independent Physician Associations (IPAs), enables providers to deliver high-quality care, efficiently with supportive local resources and technology tools that allow providers to focus more on patient care rather than administrative tasks. Astrana Health, the parent company, has over 20,000 in-network providers and manages over 1.6 million lives. This alliance extends to Arizona and Texas, signifying a significant step forward in advancing the quality and accessibility of healthcare in underserved communities across the country.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261009035219/en/

Verda Healthcare, Inc. is a Medicare Advantage (MA) Plan focusing on Pan-Asian, Hispanic, and Arab Americans living in deprived counties throughout the United States. Verda offers two plans, Verda Noble Care, an MA plan with Open Enrollment from October 15 through December 7, and Verda Noble Chronic Care, a Chronic Condition Special Needs Plan, (C-SNP) plan available year-round.

Frank Vo, President and CEO of Verda Healthcare, expressed his enthusiasm for this collaboration stating, "We’re thrilled to partner with AstranaCare Partners and especially excited to leverage Astrana’s proven experience in delivering exceptional care, with particular expertise in serving Pan-Asian and Hispanic communities. Together, we’ll be able to offer our members across Greater Houston, Texas, and Phoenix, Arizona, more culturally responsive care options.”

Jaime Melkonoff, Senior Vice President Business Development and President of AstranaCare Texas, shared her excitement about the recent partnership when she said, “Astrana’s growth in Arizona and Texas through payer partnership like the one with Verda gives our networks the ability to support additional members through these culturally focused plans. We are excited to support Verda’s vision to serve more members in a way that meets their needs beyond just medical services.”

About Verda Healthcare, Inc.

Verda Healthcare, Inc. was established in 2024 as a pioneering Medicare Advantage plan committed to innovation and patient-focused solutions. Verda aims to transform the healthcare experience for underrepresented individuals and families in diverse, ethnic communities. The firm strives for excellence and inclusivity.

www.verdahealthcare.com

About Astrana Health, Inc.

Astrana Health, Inc. (NASDAQ: ASTH) is a physician-centric, technology-powered, risk-bearing healthcare company. Leveraging our proprietary end-to-end technology solutions, Astrana Health operates an integrated healthcare delivery platform that enables providers to successfully participate in value-based care arrangements. Astrana’s goal is to empower entrepreneurial providers with the tools to deliver a higher level of care to our underserved patients in a cost-effective way, which we have done successfully for 35+ years.

data.title: Solvely.ai Makes the Case for AI That Builds Human Capability
data.description:
Solvely.ai Makes the Case for AI That Builds Human Capability

Solvely.ai Makes the Case for AI That Builds Human Capability

PR Newswire

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 10, 2026

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Solvely.ai, an applied AI company, outlined its approach to AI agents for learning: helping people build understanding and skills, rather than simply completing tasks.

Co-founder Richard Weiqi Zhang shared this perspective at Funding Conviction, a September 18, 2026, webinar on education investment and the future of learning. Hosted by Edtech Insiders, the discussion featured Reach Capital's Steve Kupfer and Minerva's Ben Nelson.

"Learning has to make the person more capable," said Zhang. "The goal is still to empower the learner, not to replace them."

Building learning-specific intelligence

To support this approach, Solvely develops its own specialized models and agent systems for learning. It uses education-domain post-training to tailor models to specific learning tasks. Its agentic system identifies instructional content in images and documents, segments individual questions and routes each problem  to the appropriate solving algorithm and visualization tools. Its agent architecture brings models, context and educational tools together to create explanations, visual exploration and practice. For problem-solving, Solvely cross-checks responses across multiple models.

An Anthropic case study shows how Solvely uses Claude to create interactive visualizations that learners can explore by changing inputs.

From answers to understanding

With Solvely's AI math solver, learners can work through text or image-based questions with step-by-step explanations, ask follow-up questions and explore problems visually through whiteboard explanations. For exam preparation, they can turn their own course materials into study guides, flashcards and quizzes for review and practice.

For writing review, its AI detector provides signals for closer examination, not proof of authorship. Its published AI-text detection research details how the company develops, fine-tunes and evaluates task-specific models. Users remain responsible for reviewing output and following applicable academic requirements.

Industry recognition

Solvely was named to Nasdaq and Notable Capital's inaugural Prosumer AI 40, alongside OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor and Lovable. It was also selected for the 2026 GSV Cup 50, recognizing 50 of the world's most promising EdTech startups.

Watch the webinar or explore Solvely.ai.

About Solvely.ai

Solvely.ai is an applied AI company amplifying human capability. Its AI agents help people learn, grow and realize their potential in the age of AI. Since launching in San Francisco in 2023, Solvely has served over 15 million users across 180+ countries.

Media contact: Richard Weiqi Zhang, richard@solvely.ai

data.title: STARMUS VIII Announces Two Young Changemakers as Junior Medal Winners
data.description:
STARMUS VIII Announces Two Young Changemakers as Junior Medal Winners

STARMUS VIII Announces Two Young Changemakers as Junior Medal Winners

PR Newswire

CANARY ISLANDS, Spain, Oct. 10, 2026

Valeria Corrales receives the Junior Stephen Hawking Medal and Aneeshwar Kunchala receives the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal

CANARY ISLANDS, Spain, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- STARMUS VIII, the premier international festival of science, music and exploration, is proud to announce the recipients of two special distinctions celebrating the next generation of scientific and environmental leaders.

Valeria Corrales, from Spain, will receive the Junior Stephen Hawking Medal, in recognition of her exceptional work bringing science, programming and technology to young audiences.

Aneeshwar Kunchala, from the United Kingdom, will receive the Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal, honouring his remarkable dedication to wildlife conservation, biodiversity and inspiring children to protect the natural world.

Although their work focuses on different fields, both young changemakers share a conviction at the heart of STARMUS: knowledge should inspire action, and age should never be a barrier to making a difference.

Valeria Corrales — Junior Stephen Hawking Medal

Valeria Corrales began her journey in science communication at the age of ten, when she co-founded the educational platform ValPat in 2018 alongside her mentor Patricia Heredia.

What began as an initiative to make science and technology more accessible has grown into a major Spanish-language STEM education platform, with more than 750 videos and 240,000 YouTube subscribers.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Valeria and Patricia offered 100 consecutive days of free online STEM classes, helping thousands of children across Spain and Latin America continue learning during lockdown.

Valeria has since received national and international recognition. She was named among Forbes Spain's 23 Changemakers in 2023, became a finalist for the Princess of Girona Social Award in 2025, and was selected as a Top 10 finalist for the Global Student Prize from nearly 11,000 applications and nominations across 148 countries.

Now studying Computational Media at the Georgia Institute of Technology, she continues to explore how science, technology, creativity and storytelling can transform education.

Her achievements reflect the spirit of Stephen Hawking's belief in the power of curiosity and the importance of sharing scientific knowledge with everyone.

Aneeshwar Kunchala — Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal

At just eleven years old, Aneeshwar Kunchala has already become an internationally recognized voice for wildlife conservation and environmental education.

His extraordinary journey began when he was only four, after learning about a whale that had died because of plastic pollution. That experience inspired a mission to protect animals and encourage others to care for the natural world.

Since then, Aneeshwar has reached international audiences through television documentaries, educational programmes, public speaking, journalism and art.

His work includes appearances and productions for BBC, Sky Kids and Channel 5, while his conservation message has reached audiences at major international events and institutions.

Aneeshwar holds three Guinness World Records and has received honours including the Diana Award and the British Citizen Youth Award. He has also been named a young ambassador for the National Trust and became the first young columnist for National Geographic Kids UK. He has also been recognized with the Young Scientific Explorer honorary award - from the Scientific Exploration Society.

His work combines scientific curiosity, compassion for animals and an extraordinary ability to communicate with younger generations.

His guiding message captures the simplicity and urgency of his mission:

"Save the animals and make sure the world looks beautiful."

The Junior Jane Goodall Earth Medal recognizes not only his achievements, but also his determination to inspire a generation that sees the protection of biodiversity as a shared responsibility.

Two Young Voices, One Shared Future

Stephen Hawking dedicated his life to understanding the Universe. Jane Goodall transformed our understanding of the natural world and our responsibility to protect it.

Through these two Junior Medals, STARMUS celebrates the continuation of their legacies in a new generation.

Valeria Corrales is helping young people discover the power of science and technology. Aneeshwar Kunchala is inspiring them to protect the extraordinary diversity of life on our planet.

Together, they represent a powerful message: the future of science and the future of our planet belong to those who are curious enough to ask questions and courageous enough to act.

The awards will be presented during STARMUS VIII, taking place in Tenerife and La Palma, Canary Islands, from 17 to 22 October 2026, under the theme The Search for Truth. The Festival will bring together some of the world's leading figures in science, space exploration, technology, music and the arts to explore the importance of evidence, knowledge, reason and scientific thinking in an increasingly complex world.

data.title: 'I feel like a loser': My stock portfolio is swinging wildly. Is it finally time to worry?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'I presume these are sophisticated investors taking a profit'

"I haven't made any money in months." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm frustrated with the stock market. One day, my exchange-traded funds go up the next day, and the next day they crash. I presume these are sophisticated investors taking a profit. I haven't made any money in months. No yield at all. What to do? I feel like a loser. It would have been nice to be able to get a yield. Is anyone else having this experience? What strategies do you suggest for someone who is slowly and gratefully heading toward retirement?

Retail Investor

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I'm never selling': I'm 47 and buy bitcoin with every dollar I earn. Am I crazy?

ADHD is on the rise, which mental-health experts attribute, at least in part, to our personal technology.

Dear Investor,

ETFs are traded throughout the day, but transparency does not equate to volatility.

Yes, they will fluctuate on any given day, week or month, as the news cycle pushes and pulls your stocks three ways from Friday. Yield, for the record, is also different from return; it represents the income generated - like interest and dividends - while return refers to the overall net gain/loss. Technology is all turning us all into checkaholics. We're up there with chocoholics. We want instant gratification, whether it's a boost of dopamine from checking ETFs, or a sugar rush from eating candy. If checking your portfolio is making you anxious rather than helping you make better decisions, STOP checking your accounts.

Focus instead on the long-term trajectory, which historically has tended to rise over decades. Forget about investors making money off microtrades. You don't need to beat those investors. Forget about them; they have nothing to do with you. Checking daily moves in your accounts gives you an inaccurate or, at the very least, incomplete outlook about the stock market's overall health. Here's a reality check. The S&P 500 SPX has risen roughly 14% from January to October, the Nasdaq COMP composite has increased by 18%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA has risen by more than 6% and the Russell 2000 RUT has increased by 13%.

Your anxieties are understandable. Tech and AI stocks are driving the majority of gains in the U.S. stock market. The geopolitical backdrop - the war in Iran, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war - has spooked investors and led to fears of a recession, none of which have come to fruition. As you get older, the share of your portfolio invested in stocks typically changes to reflect the time you have to recover from a major correction in the markets (the "sequence of return" risk). That risk is particularly important in the years just before and after retirement: A large market decline early in retirement can damage your portfolio more than a similar decline happening many years later.

Don't miss: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?

Seeking safety

A few broad strokes: Explore CDs and high-yield savings accounts (HYSAs) for safety, but you may have to sacrifice higher returns. Treasury securities and high-quality bonds can also play a role. You say you are concerned about yield/return. That's understandable. In that case, you should decide how much of your portfolio you want to devote to predictable income, especially if you're upset by the movements in your account, and how much you still need to invest for long-term growth so you can enjoy a comfortable retirement.

There are also psychological and behavioral reasons why incessant checking of your portfolio occurs - and why it can be counterproductive. Loss aversion, a term popularized by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, describes the tendency for people to experience the stress of a financial loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent return on your investment. As a result, you may be inadvertently conditioning yourself to constantly monitor your Robinhood, Vanguard or Fidelity accounts. It's a toxic feedback loop!

Possibly of more interest to you, given your obsessive checking of our own portfolio: Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler developed the concept of "myopic loss aversion," suggesting that the more often you check your portfolios, the more likely you are to notice short-term declines and also react emotionally to them. That's why people sell their stocks in a panic during a market correction and/or go heavy in gold, dive headfirst into bonds and cash vehicles instead, only to regret it later. Don't make a decision on Thursday because of what happened on Wednesday.

Don't miss: 'I'd rather be on a beach in Bali': My husband resents my $8 million net worth. Should I pay for his retirement?

Risk perception

Since you ask about strategies for alleviating risk or the perception of risk: First, take stock of what you actually own and when you'll need the money. If you're overly concerned about short-term movements in your portfolio, you could employ a dollar-cost-averaging strategy, where you divide the amount to be invested in vehicles - be they Treasuries or CDs - into equal-size contributions and invest them over a longer period. Dollar-cost averaging, for example, can make sense when you're investing new money and want to reduce the psychological discomfort of investing a lump sum.

A "bond-tent strategy" involves gradually exposing your portfolio's allocation to bonds in the years leading up to retirement, keeping a higher bond allocation early after retiring and gradually lowering that exposure later. The idea is to create a buffer against needing to sell stocks after a major market decline early, especially early in retirement. It can reduce your sequence-of-returns risk. As long as you have enough money to live on, plus a 12-month emergency fund, it's also worth figuring out how long your retirement savings will have to last and how much you expect to withdraw each year.

A "bond ladder" of individual CDs or bonds, on the other hand, matures at different times and can provide a more predictable income stream while reducing the need to sell investments at a bad time and reducing exposure to interest-rate and stock-market moves. A ladder can be useful if you know roughly when you'll need the money. Whatever you choose, your portfolio should have an age-appropriate mix of stocks and bonds, and cash equivalents. The right mix depends on your spending needs, other sources of income, your time horizon and - yes - your tolerance for risk.

Constant checking creates unnecessary drama. Sometimes, it's better to pick up a good book.

Related: I'm 71 and still working. I earn $108,000 a year. Am I doing the right thing?
